section.title: Wisdom and Folly
section.sectionRationale: The Teacher gathers a string of proverbs that trace how folly works. A little foolishness can ruin much, like dead flies in perfume; folly is exalted while the worthy are lowered; the fool's own words consume him; laziness lets the roof cave in. Beneath the seemingly scattered sayings runs one theme: how folly quietly unravels a life and a land, and how wisdom, patient and skillful, holds them together.
section.thesis: A little folly outweighs much wisdom and honor, and the Teacher's proverbs show folly at work at every level, in speech, labor, government, and the heart, quietly undoing what wisdom builds; the wise are marked by calm skill, restraint, and diligence, while the fool broadcasts his emptiness and consumes himself with his own words.
section.frameNote: Four movements: a little folly that outweighs wisdom and honor; the world turned upside down when folly is set on high; the hazards and skill of work and the fool's self consuming speech; and woe to the land whose leaders feast recklessly, ending with the warning that even your private words may take wing.

units.label: A little folly outweighs wisdom
units.note: how folly ruins out of all proportion

verses.text: As dead flies bring a stench to the perfumer’s oil, so a little folly outweighs {{chokmah|wisdom}} and honor.
A wise man’s heart inclines to the right, but the heart of a {{kesil|fool}} to the left.
Even as the fool walks along the road, his sense is lacking, and he shows everyone that he is a {{sakal|fool}}.
If the ruler’s temper flares against you, do not abandon your post, for calmness lays great offenses to rest.

units.label: The world turned upside down
units.note: folly set on high, the worthy brought low

verses.text: There is an evil I have seen under the sun, an error that proceeds from the ruler:
Folly is appointed to great heights, but the rich sit in lowly positions.
I have seen slaves on horseback, while princes go on foot like slaves.

units.label: Skill, snares, and the fool's words
units.note: the hazards of work and self consuming speech

verses.text: He who digs a pit may fall into it, and he who breaches a wall may be bitten by a snake.
The one who quarries stones may be injured by them, and he who splits logs endangers himself.
If the axe is dull and the blade unsharpened, more strength must be exerted, but skill produces success.
If the snake bites before it is charmed, there is no profit for the charmer.
The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious, but the lips of a {{kesil|fool}} consume him.
The beginning of his talk is folly, and the end of his speech is evil madness.
Yet the {{sakal|fool}} multiplies words. No one knows what is coming, and who can tell him what will come after him?
The toil of a fool wearies him, for he does not know the way to the city.

units.label: Woe to the land, and the reach of your words
units.note: folly unravels a land and a life

verses.text: Woe to you, O land whose king is a youth, and whose princes feast in the morning.
Blessed are you, O land whose king is a son of nobles, and whose princes feast at the proper time, for strength and not for drunkenness.
Through laziness the roof caves in, and in the hands of the idle, the house leaks.
A feast is prepared for laughter, and wine makes life merry, but money is the answer for everything.
Do not curse the king even in your thoughts, or curse the rich even in your bedroom, for a bird of the air may carry your words, and a winged creature may report your speech.

chokmah.gloss: Wisdom, skill for living well. In this chapter wisdom is the patient, practical competence that sharpens the axe, speaks with grace, and keeps a life and a land in order, so precious that even a little folly can outweigh it, as dead flies spoil good perfume.

kesil.gloss: A fool, the dull and self assured kind who despises wisdom. In Ecclesiastes 10 the kesil's heart leans the wrong way, and his own lips consume him, so that his folly works its ruin from the inside out.

sakal.gloss: A fool, marked by a lack of sense that shows itself openly. The sakal broadcasts his folly to everyone on the road and multiplies empty words, wearying himself with toil because he does not even know the way to the city.

basic.context: This chapter is a collection of proverbs, and at first it can feel like a scattering of unrelated sayings. But a single concern runs through them: how folly works, and how wisdom answers it. A little folly, the Teacher says, can undo a great deal of wisdom and honor, the way a few dead flies ruin a jar of expensive perfume. He watches folly get promoted while worthy people are pushed down, notes the everyday hazards of work and the value of sharpened skill, and describes how the fool's own mouth destroys him, beginning in nonsense and ending in dangerous madness. He warns that a lazy household falls apart and that reckless leaders bring woe on a whole land. He closes with a shrewd caution: guard even your private words, for they have a way of taking wing.
basic.hermeneutics: Proverbs like these are general truths about how life usually goes, not ironclad promises. They observe patterns: skill tends to succeed, calm defuses anger, folly tends to expose and consume itself. They are meant to train the instincts, not to be applied mechanically. Read this way, the chapter is not random at all; it is a coherent portrait of folly's slow unraveling of a life and a land, set against the quiet competence of wisdom. The counsel about rulers is practical shrewdness for living under power, not a theology of the state.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter turns on three words. Chokmah, wisdom, is the practical skill that sharpens the axe, speaks with grace, and holds life together; it is so valuable that a little folly can outweigh it. Two words are used for the fool: the kesil, the dull and self assured fool whose own lips consume him, and the sakal, the senseless fool who broadcasts his emptiness on the road and wearies himself with toil.
basic.typology: The proverbs long for a wisdom that truly orders life and a rule that blesses rather than curses the land. Both point beyond Solomon's court. The wisdom that produces success and speaks with grace anticipates Christ, the wisdom of God, whose words are always gracious. And the blessed land whose king is nobly born and whose rule brings strength points to the kingdom of the true King, born of David's line, under whom the world is finally set right side up.
basic.christ: The fool's mouth begins in folly and ends in madness and consumes him; by contrast the words of the wise are gracious, a description fulfilled in Christ, of whom it was said that no one ever spoke like this man and that gracious words came from His lips. Where this chapter grieves that folly is exalted and the worthy brought low, Christ is the worthy One who was brought lowest of all and then exalted to the highest place, and who will finally reverse every folly enthroned. He is the wisdom of God in whom life and the world are at last rightly ordered.
basic.god: God stands behind the moral order these proverbs describe: the world is made so that wisdom, skill, restraint, and diligence tend to build, while folly, laziness, and reckless speech tend to destroy. He is not named in every saying, but He is the one who has woven this grain into life, and the fear of Him, established earlier in the book, is the root of the wisdom these proverbs commend.
basic.crossReferences: The book of Proverbs runs parallel throughout, especially on the fool's speech and the sluggard's ruin. James 3 develops the danger of the tongue. Luke 4 records that gracious words came from Christ's lips. Philippians 2 shows the worthy One brought low and then exalted, the great reversal these proverbs await.
basic.oneStory: Ecclesiastes 10 shows a world where folly keeps climbing and wisdom keeps being overlooked, a world subjected to frustration and waiting to be set right. The Teacher can only describe the pattern and commend the better way of wisdom. The story moves on to Christ, the wisdom of God and the worthy King, who was brought low and then exalted, and who will one day turn the upside down world the right way up in His kingdom.

context.literary:
Read slowly, chapter 10 has a spine. It opens by taking up the last line of chapter 9, 'one sinner destroys much good,' and giving it a picture: a few flies in a perfumer's oil. It then moves outward in widening circles. Verses 1 to 3 are about the individual heart, with the right and left hand as the two directions it can lean. Verses 4 to 7 move to the court, where a ruler's temper and the promotion of fools show folly at the top. Verses 8 to 11 step down to the workplace, with four small proverbs about the hazards of digging, quarrying, splitting logs and charming snakes, and one about skill. Verses 12 to 15 return to the fool's mouth. Verses 16 and 17 give a woe and a blessing for a whole land. Verses 18 to 20 close in the household and the bedroom, with a leaking roof, a feast, and a whisper.

The shape runs from the heart to the road, the court, the work site, the mouth, the nation, the house, and finally the private thought. Nowhere is life safe from folly, and nowhere is it out of reach of wisdom.

Several verses are built on contrasts. The 'right' and 'left' of verse 2 are opposites. The 'woe' of verse 16 is balanced by the 'blessed' of verse 17, the word that opens Psalm 1. The mouth of the wise is 'gracious' while the lips of the fool 'consume him,' verse 12. The fool's speech has a 'beginning' and an 'end' in verse 13, folly at the start and evil madness at the close, so that the proverb has a downward slope inside it. The sayings in verses 8 to 9 share a single device: each worker causes his own harm, the one who digs falls in, the one who quarries is hurt by the stone.

The chapter also contains one longer observation, verses 5 to 7, introduced as 'an evil I have seen under the sun,' the same formula as elsewhere in the book. That marks it as the Teacher's own report and not one more traditional saying.
context.historical:
Many of these sayings assume a royal court. 'The wrath of a king is a messenger of death, but a wise man will pacify it,' says Proverbs 16:14, and Ecclesiastes 10:4 gives the same advice in other words: stay at your post and keep calm. An official who ran or exploded could make a bad matter worse. The inversions of verses 6 and 7, folly on high, slaves riding horses and princes walking, would have been shocking in a society where the horse was a mark of rank. Proverbs 30:21-22 lists 'a servant who becomes king' among the things that make the earth tremble, Proverbs 19:10 calls it unseemly for a slave to rule over princes, and Isaiah 3:4 threatens that God will make 'mere lads their leaders.'

Verse 16 has a counterpart in Isaiah 5:11, 'Woe to those who rise early in the morning in pursuit of strong drink.' Feasting in the morning was a sign of leaders who had no thought for the day's work, and the apostles' defence on the day of Pentecost, 'It is only the third hour of the day,' shows that no one expected honest people to be drunk at that hour, Acts 2:15. Proverbs 31:4-5 warns that kings who drink 'forget what is decreed, depriving all the oppressed of justice.'

The work proverbs speak of ordinary risks. Pits were dug as cisterns and for trapping, and stone walls had crevices where snakes lived, which fits Amos 5:19, where a man leans his hand on his wall and is bitten. Quarrying and log splitting are dangerous trades. The snake charmer is a recognised figure in Psalm 58:4-5, where a cobra refuses the charmer's tune. A flat mud roof needed regular maintenance, and 'a constant dripping' is a byword for domestic misery, Proverbs 19:13.

The closing warning about cursing the king, even in a bedroom, reflects a world of courtiers and informers. Israel's own law already forbade it: 'You must not blaspheme God or curse the ruler of your people,' Exodus 22:28.
context.canonical:
This is the most Proverbs-like chapter in the book, and several sayings have direct counterparts in that book: the self-ruining mouth of the fool in Proverbs 18:6-7, the pit that catches the digger in Proverbs 26:27, the sluggard whose property falls to ruin in Proverbs 24:30-34. It is a reminder that Ecclesiastes is not the enemy of wisdom literature; it is a voice within it that insists on honesty about the limits of wisdom while still prizing the thing.

The chapter has a quiet irony in its place in the canon. Solomon, the king of 1 Kings 4:29-30, whose wisdom exceeded that of all the men of the East, is the one who, 'when Solomon grew old,' saw his wives turn his heart away, 1 Kings 11:4. A little folly outweighed much wisdom in the house of the wisest king. The woe over a land whose rulers are unfit, verse 16, also finds echoes in the prophets, as in Isaiah 3:4.

The New Testament takes the teaching on the tongue much further. James takes up the small member that sets a great forest ablaze, James 3:5-10, and Jesus teaches that 'for every careless word' people will give an account, Matthew 12:36-37, and that what is whispered in the inner rooms will be proclaimed from the housetops, Luke 12:2-3, which reads like a divine commentary on the bird that carries a secret in verse 20. Paul himself quotes Exodus 22:28 when he realises he has spoken sharply to the high priest, Acts 23:5. The longing for a blessed land under a just king looks forward to Isaiah 32:1 and ultimately to Christ.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The Teacher wanted his students to see folly as something with a pattern, so that they could spot it early. Folly does not announce itself; it begins in the heart's leaning, shows on the road in an unguarded sentence, and grows in speech until it ends in what verse 13 calls evil madness. He wanted young men who would enter public life to know how to behave under a hot-tempered ruler, to stay at their posts and keep their heads, and not to be undone by cynicism when fools rise.

He also meant them to take craft seriously. Four of the proverbs concern the practical skill of the worker, and verse 10 says the person who sharpens the blade does less work for more result. Wisdom is not only about moral choices; it is about doing things well. And he meant to warn them about speech. The chapter closes on the thought that words travel, and that the room where a thing is whispered is not as private as it looks.

For a nation, the chapter is a plea to look at who is leading. For an individual, it is a call to guard the heart, the mouth and the work. The hearer is not told that wisdom always wins, since the same chapter has the worthy sitting low. He is told that wisdom is still the better road.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of the chapter is description in proverb form, and proverbs state how things usually go, not how they must. Verse 10 does not promise that sharpening an axe will always save effort; it observes that a dull blade costs more strength. Verses 6 and 7 describe an inversion the Teacher has seen and calls an evil. He does not recommend it, and it would be a mistake to read it as his approval of folly in the high places.

A few verses are advice. 'Do not abandon your post' in verse 4 is a counsel for a bad moment with a superior. 'Do not curse the king even in your thoughts' in verse 20 is a command, and it matches the earlier law. Verse 19 is the hardest. It states, 'money is the answer for everything,' as something people say or find, and it sits oddly beside the warnings around it. It should be read as an observation and not as a recommendation.

Applying the chapter today means three things. Guard speech as a skill of wisdom, including speech about leaders in private. Value competence and preparation without turning them into a guarantee. And pray for and prepare for leaders, remembering that Paul says authorities are appointed by God, Romans 13:1, while Scripture is also frank that rulers can be fools.

debates.question: Is the chapter a loose heap of proverbs or a planned portrait of folly?

views.label: A loose anthology
views.case: The topics shift quickly, from flies to rulers to snakes to roofs, and few verses are linked by an explicit connecting word. Proverb collections elsewhere often gather sayings by catchword, and this chapter may be one more such gathering.

views.label: A deliberate portrait
views.case: The chapter starts with the last line of chapter 9, moves outward from heart to court to workplace to mouth to nation to household, and ends with the private word. Repeated words such as fool, wise, heart, mouth and ruler tie the parts together, and the sayings are chosen to show folly in every setting.

debates.bearing: The truth may lie in between: a collection arranged with enough care to carry a theme. Reading it as a portrait is the more fruitful path, because it lets each saying throw light on its neighbours without forcing a single argument onto a form that does not always have one.

debates.question: Why does the Teacher counsel respect for a ruler even in private thoughts, verse 20?

views.label: Prudence in a dangerous court
views.case: The reasoning given is practical: 'a bird of the air may carry your words.' In a world of informers, one careless remark about the king or the rich could cost a person everything. On this view the verse is worldly wisdom about survival.

views.label: A principle of honouring authority
views.case: The command echoes Exodus 22:28 and the New Testament's teaching, Romans 13:1 and 1 Peter 2:17. On this view the bird is only the practical reason added to a principled command that the people of God do not curse the ruler of their people.

debates.bearing: The verse can carry both at once. The Teacher gives a prudential reason for a principle that the law had already set. It still leaves room for honest, public speech against injustice, as the prophets show; what it rules out is the secret curse and the bitter heart.

debates.question: What is the point of verse 19, 'money is the answer for everything'?

views.label: A cynical saying the Teacher reports
views.case: Set between a verse on feasting and a warning about cursing the rich, the line reads like a popular saying that expresses how the world works. The Teacher records it as a true observation of what money can do, without endorsing it as the final truth.

views.label: A sober piece of practical wisdom
views.case: Money does answer many needs, from the feast to the roof repair. The Teacher elsewhere says that 'wisdom, like money, is a shelter,' Ecclesiastes 7:12, and does not scorn wealth when it is received as God's gift.

debates.bearing: Either way the sentence is not the book's last word on wealth, which says that money cannot satisfy, Ecclesiastes 5:10, and that its enjoyment is a gift, 5:19. Read it as an observation that needs the rest of the book to be kept in check.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 has a small piece of vividness in the Hebrew. The 'dead flies' are literally flies of death, and the verbs describing what they do to the oil are two: it stinks and it ferments, as if the whole jar turns. The 'outweighs' of the second half plays on the word for honour, kavod, whose root means heavy. A little folly is weightier than wisdom and honor together, the way a small thing on one pan of a scale can tip the balance.

In verse 2 the 'heart,' lev, is the Hebrew word for the mind and will as much as for feeling. The wise man's heart goes to the right, the favoured side, and the fool's to the left. So the statement is not about emotion but about direction of thought, and in verse 3 it is the lack of this heart, his 'sense,' that the fool broadcasts on the road.

In verse 4 'calmness,' marpe, is from the root of healing, rapha. It is the same word as the 'tranquil heart' of Proverbs 14:30 and the healing tongue of the wise in Proverbs 12:18. Calm is a medicine. The verb 'lays to rest' comes from the root meaning rest, so the picture is that calm puts great offences to bed.

In verse 10 the word translated 'success' comes from a root meaning to succeed or be fit, and the 'advantage' it describes belongs to the book's key economic word yitron, the gain the Teacher asked about in 1:3. The same word appears in verse 11, 'no profit for the charmer.' Here at last is a gain that can be had, though a modest one: the profit of skill.

In verse 12 the speech of the wise is 'gracious,' chen, grace or favour, the word that in Psalm 45:2 anoints a king's lips with 'grace.' The fool's lips 'consume him,' from bala, to swallow, so that the mouth that should give grace swallows its owner. The 'madness' of verse 13 is holelot, the same word used in 9:3 for what fills human hearts while they live. The fool's talk ends where the human heart already is.

Verse 16 says 'king whose is a youth,' na'ar, and the BSB footnote says 'or a servant.' The word covers a boy, a young man and an attendant, which is why Solomon could say of himself 'I am only a little child,' 1 Kings 3:7. The inexperience, not age, is what the proverb fears. The blessing in verse 17 is ashrey, the word that opens Psalm 1. Verse 20 calls the bird a 'winged creature,' and the Hebrew idiom is literally an owner of wings.

typology.type: The wise man whose words are gracious, 10:12
typology.fulfillment: The Teacher's wise man is a pattern, and Christ is the person. The Messiah's lips were anointed with grace, Psalm 45:2, and at Nazareth 'all spoke well of Him and marveled at the gracious words that came from His lips,' Luke 4:22. Even officers sent to arrest Him returned saying no one had ever spoken as He did, and Peter confessed 'You have the words of eternal life,' John 6:68. The type falls short in that the wise man's graciousness is learned and fragile; His is perfect, and His words give life, not only good counsel.

typology.type: Folly on high and the worthy brought low, 10:6-7
typology.fulfillment: At the trial of Jesus the crowd asked that a murderer be released and the Holy and Righteous One be put to death, Acts 3:14-15. Folly was lifted high and the worthy was set at the lowest place. The Teacher mourned that inversion. The gospel does not remove it but transforms it: the One brought lowest, 'to death on a cross,' was then exalted 'to the highest place,' Philippians 2:8-9. The inversion of verses 6 and 7 is reversed by the cross and resurrection and will be fully set right at His return.

typology.type: The perfumer's oil spoiled by flies, 10:1
typology.fulfillment: Folly spoils the fragrance of a good life. In the Gospels it is reversed. When Mary poured out costly perfume on Jesus' feet, 'the house was filled with the fragrance,' John 12:3, and Paul says believers are 'to God the sweet aroma of Christ,' 2 Corinthians 2:15. Christ Himself was 'a fragrant sacrificial offering to God,' Ephesians 5:2. Where a little folly could taint everything, the fragrance of Christ spreads everywhere. The type falls short only because the Teacher's oil is at risk, while Christ's offering cannot be spoiled.

typology.type: The blessed land whose king is a son of nobles, 10:17
typology.fulfillment: A land is blessed when its ruler is fit and its princes feast at the proper time 'for strength and not for drunkenness.' Isaiah promises 'a king will reign in righteousness, and princes will rule with justice,' Isaiah 32:1, and Gabriel promises that the throne of David will be given to Jesus, whose 'kingdom will never end,' Luke 1:32-33. At the supper Jesus Himself looks ahead to drinking the cup new in His Father's kingdom, Matthew 26:29. The Teacher can only bless the land that has such a king; Christ is the king the blessing is waiting for.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ most plainly by the person of the wise man. The Teacher offers a portrait of someone whose words are gracious, whose calm heals, whose skill produces results and whose heart leans right. Paul says Christ 'has become for us wisdom from God,' 1 Corinthians 1:30, and that in Him 'are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,' Colossians 2:3. The Spirit of wisdom and counsel rests on the coming Branch, Isaiah 11:1-2. The crowds in the synagogue asked, 'Where did this man get such wisdom?' Matthew 13:54, and Jesus Himself pointed out that 'One greater than Solomon is here,' Matthew 12:42. The wisest king of Israel became the standing example of how wisdom can be undone, 1 Kings 11:4. Christ is wisdom that cannot be undone.

It leads to Christ by His conduct before power. Verse 4 advises that when a ruler's temper flares, a person should not leave his post, because calmness settles great offences. Before Pilate, Jesus is calm and unafraid. When told that Pilate had authority to release or crucify, He answered that Pilate would have no authority unless it were given from above, John 19:10-11. When people 'heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate,' but 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23. He did not abandon His post, and in doing so He did what the proverb could only recommend.

It leads to Christ by the inversion of verses 6 and 7. At the trial the crowd asked for the release of Barabbas, a murderer, and the Righteous One was sent to the cross, Acts 3:14-15. That is folly on high in its starkest form. The Teacher can say only that it is an evil he has seen. The gospel says that God used even this to exalt the One who was brought low, Philippians 2:8-11, and Mary's song promised that He 'has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble,' Luke 1:52.

It leads to Christ finally by the longing in verse 17 for a ruler who is fit for rule. Isaiah's king will 'judge the poor with righteousness,' Isaiah 11:4, and 'of the increase of His government and peace there will be no end,' Isaiah 9:7. The Teacher cannot name this king. He can say what the blessing of his land would be.

A caution is in order. These proverbs are not riddles about Jesus, and the dead flies, the snake and the roof are not hidden pictures of Him. The links rest on the larger themes of wisdom, gracious speech, and just rule, which the New Testament itself applies to Christ. The chapter is a portrait of what wisdom looks like, and the Gospels show who embodies it.
study.god:
The proverbs of this chapter assume that the world has a grain, and Scripture says who put it there: 'The LORD founded the earth by wisdom and established the heavens by understanding,' Proverbs 3:19. The pit digger falls into his own pit and the dull blade costs more strength because the world was made by wisdom and answers to it. God is not named in chapter 10 as often as in other chapters, but He is the one behind the order the sayings describe.

He is also the source of skill. Verse 10 praises the one who sharpens his blade. In the Bible, craft is a gift. God filled Bezalel 'with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship,' Exodus 31:3, and Isaiah says of the farmer who ploughs and sows rightly, 'his God instructs and teaches him properly,' Isaiah 28:26. A wise worker is receiving something from God, and wisdom is something to be asked for: 'If any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault,' James 1:5.

God is the one who sets up and brings down. The Teacher sees slaves on horseback and princes on foot and calls it evil, but Hannah's song says 'He humbles and He exalts,' 1 Samuel 2:7, and Mary's, 'He has brought down rulers from their thrones,' Luke 1:52. The reversal that the Teacher grieves is not outside God's reach. The tension is real, since Scripture says rulers are appointed by God, Romans 13:1, and also that He judges them, as Isaiah 3 does. The chapter does not resolve it. It teaches the reader to live wisely in the meantime.

God sees what is said in secret. The bird that carries a word, verse 20, is a picture, and the reality behind it is that 'nothing in all creation is hidden from God's sight,' Hebrews 4:13. Jesus said that what is whispered in the inner rooms will be proclaimed from the housetops, Luke 12:2-3. This is a reason for fear and also for comfort, since the same God hears prayer in secret.

He is the God who values the faithful use of the mouth. Words are a creation of His, and speech is for blessing. The wise man's gracious words reflect the God who 'gives generously' and whose own words 'are spirit and life,' as the fool's reflect nothing.

For worship, the chapter calls for humility about our own wisdom. The only safeguard against a little folly outweighing a lot of wisdom is dependence on the God who gives wisdom and who forgives its failures.

crossReferences.note: 'He who digs a pit will fall into it.' It is the proverb behind Ecclesiastes 10:8, and the lesson is the same: the dangers of one's own trade fall back on the person who works carelessly. Together they teach that harm often arrives by the road we ourselves prepared.

'Speaking rashly is like a piercing sword, but the tongue of the wise brings healing.' The healing here shares its root with the calm of Ecclesiastes 10:4. In both places wisdom is a kind of medicine, and wise speech lays hurts to rest.

A fool's lips bring strife, and his mouth is his ruin and 'a snare to his soul.' It sets out the same self-destroying mouth as Ecclesiastes 10:12-14, from the standpoint of the harm that comes to others and to himself.

The earth trembles under 'a servant who becomes king, a fool who is filled with food.' These are the same upside down arrangements that Ecclesiastes 10:6-7 sees in the court, and the proverb shows the matter was a traditional concern of Israel's sages.

'Woe to those who rise early in the morning in pursuit of strong drink.' It is the prophetic counterpart to Ecclesiastes 10:16. A land is blessed or cursed by what its leaders do with their mornings, whether they give them to drink or to just rule.

'You must not blaspheme God or curse the ruler of your people.' The law lies behind Ecclesiastes 10:20. Paul quotes it in Acts 23:5, which shows that the principle outlived the court of Israel and applies when the ruler is hostile.

Jesus says that what is said in the dark will be heard in the daylight, and what is whispered in the inner rooms will be proclaimed from the housetops. It reads as a divine commentary on the bird of the air in Ecclesiastes 10:20, but with a warning about God's judgment, not a king's informers.

People will give an account for every careless word, and by their words they will be acquitted or condemned. The fool's lips in Ecclesiastes 10:12-13 are taken up here with an eternal weight, and the way the heart shows in speech is made a matter of judgment.

The tongue is a small member that sets a great forest ablaze, and no man can tame it. James develops the Teacher's observation that a fool's words begin as folly and end as evil madness, and he adds the thought that only grace can tame what we cannot.

God has 'brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble.' It is the answer to Ecclesiastes 10:6-7. What the Teacher saw as a wrong in a world under the sun, the Magnificat sings as the work of God coming in the Messiah.

In his old age Solomon's wives turned his heart after other gods. The wisest king is the case in point of Ecclesiastes 10:1, where a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor, and a reminder that wisdom needs a heart that stays loyal to the Lord.

Believers are the sweet aroma of Christ among those being saved and those perishing. It reverses the image of Ecclesiastes 10:1: the fragrance that spreads is not spoiled by flies but is God's own, though to some it is an odor of death.

study.oneStory:
The first folly in the Bible was a heard word. The woman and the man listened to a voice that called God's word into doubt, and one small act weighed more than all the goodness around it. Genesis 3 is the great case of what Ecclesiastes 10:1 describes, a little folly outweighing wisdom and honour. The dead flies in the oil of the human race have been working ever since, in the cities of Genesis 4 to 11, in the Judges when 'everyone did what was right in his own eyes,' and in the kings.

The history of Israel's rulers is the history of verses 16 and 17 played out. Solomon's own wisdom was overcome by a heart that drifted, 1 Kings 11:4. The prophets lament the leaders who feast and forget the poor, Isaiah 5:11 and Isaiah 3:4, and the exile is the woe of a land with unfit rulers. Wisdom is also a thread in the story: Proverbs praises the wisdom by which 'the LORD founded the earth,' Proverbs 3:19, and invites us to walk with her.

The Teacher stands in the middle of this story. He describes folly truly and cannot cure it. The promise of a ruler who will 'judge the poor with righteousness,' Isaiah 11:4, is the longing in the background of the blessing of verse 17. When Christ comes, He is the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24, and the King who is greater than Solomon, Matthew 12:42. He is brought low by folly on the cross and raised high by God, Philippians 2:8-11, and so the inversion of verses 6 and 7 is turned the right way up.

His people live now as those who ask for wisdom, James 1:5, who guard their mouths, who work well, and who pray for rulers while they wait for the true one. The end of the story takes the curse out of the land: 'No longer will there be any curse,' and the leaves of the tree of life are 'for the healing of the nations,' Revelation 22:2-3. In that city the King rules in righteousness and there is no more folly in the court, no more dead fly in the oil, and no more word that must be whispered. The wise reign of the Lamb is what the sayings of this chapter have been leaning toward.

quiz.q: What does the image of dead flies in the perfumer's oil teach?

options.text: A little folly can outweigh much wisdom and honor, spoiling the whole.
options.note: Small folly ruins out of all proportion, like flies spoiling good perfume.

options.text: That perfume should be kept carefully sealed.
options.note: The image is a metaphor for folly's disproportionate damage, not advice on perfume.

options.text: Even small foolish acts can undermine a reputation built on wisdom.
options.note: A fair application of the proverb to honor and reputation.

options.text: That wisdom and folly are basically equal in value.
options.note: The proverb prizes wisdom highly; that is why a little folly is so costly.

quiz.q: How does the fool reveal himself, according to the chapter?

options.text: His own lips consume him; his talk begins in folly and ends in madness, and he multiplies words.
options.note: The fool's self exposing, self destroying speech is a central theme.

options.text: By staying completely silent at all times.
options.note: The opposite; the fool multiplies words and broadcasts his folly.

options.text: He shows his lack of sense to everyone, even as he walks along the road.
options.note: True to verse 3, though the sharpest picture is his self consuming speech.

options.text: By always sharpening his tools before working.
options.note: Sharpening the axe is the mark of wise skill, not of the fool.

quiz.q: What is the best way to read this chapter's string of proverbs?

options.text: As a coherent portrait of how folly unravels a life and a land, set against wisdom's quiet skill.
options.note: Beneath the variety runs one sustained theme of folly at work.

options.text: As a random, meaningless list with no connection at all.
options.note: The sayings share a clear underlying subject, folly and wisdom.

options.text: As varied sayings held together by the recurring figures of fool, ruler, and worker.
options.note: A reasonable read that notices the unifying figures.

options.text: As strict promises that always come true without exception.
options.note: Proverbs are general truths that shape instincts, not ironclad guarantees.

quiz.q: What does the counsel about the ruler's anger and cursing the king teach?

options.text: Practical shrewdness under power: keep calm, hold your post, and guard even your private words.
options.note: Calm defuses offense, and careless words have a way of taking wing.

options.text: That you should flee any ruler the moment he is displeased.
options.note: The proverb says the opposite; do not abandon your post.

options.text: That restraint and discretion protect you where rash reaction would harm you.
options.note: A good summary of the chapter's prudence under authority.

options.text: That rulers can never hear what is said about them.
options.note: The point is the reverse; even a bird may carry your words.

quiz.q: How does the chapter point forward to Christ?

options.text: The worthy brought low then exalted, and the gracious words of the wise, find their fulfillment in Christ.
options.note: Christ is the humbled and exalted worthy One and the wisdom of God whose speech is gracious.

options.text: It offers no connection to Christ, being only practical advice.
options.note: Its longing for wise rule and gracious speech is answered in Christ.

options.text: The blessed land whose king is nobly born anticipates the kingdom of the true King.
options.note: A genuine typology pointing to Christ's reign.

options.text: It predicts the political history of Israel's monarchy in detail.
options.note: The chapter gives wisdom, not detailed political prophecy.

questions: A little folly can outweigh much wisdom and honor. Where might a small, tolerated foolishness be quietly undermining something good you have built?
The words of the wise are gracious, but the fool's lips consume him. What would it look like for your speech this week to give grace rather than to run on and harm?
Calmness lays great offenses to rest. Where are you tempted to react hotly under someone's anger, and how might steady calm serve you and others better?
The Teacher praised skill: a sharpened axe succeeds where brute force wearies. Where are you pushing with raw effort when patient skill or preparation is what is needed?

The chapter grieves a world where folly is exalted and the worthy are brought low. How does it steady you to know that Christ, the worthy One, was humbled and then exalted, and will set the world right?

translationNotes.note: Wisdom renders chokmah, the practical skill for living well; the proverb sets its great value against the small amount of folly that can spoil it, like dead flies in perfume.
Fool here renders kesil, the dull and self assured fool whose heart leans the wrong way and whose own lips consume him.
Fool here renders sakal, the senseless fool who openly shows his lack of judgment and multiplies empty words.
Under the sun frames the Teacher's observation of a disordered world where folly is exalted and the worthy brought low, an evil awaiting the setting right of God's kingdom.
